terms.gloss: a label, a ticket: here, a price tag
evidence: Petr. 34: pittacia erant affīxa cum hōc titulō
terms.comment: Classically a slip of parchment or a ticket fastened to a thing, such as the labels on Trimalchio’s wine jars (Lewis & Short). Its use for the ticket that shows a price is modern, and ours. It is the word this lexicon uses for a label on food (see “best-before date”).

terms.gloss: a ticket, bill, or notice that a thing is for sale
evidence: Plin. Ep. 7.27.7: lēgit titulum audītōque pretiō
Levi–Bini p. 25: nota, praescrīptiō, titulus, for a label
terms.comment: Lewis & Short’s word for the notice put up on a house that was for sale or to let; see “sign”.

phrases.english: How much is it? Look at the price tag.
The price is on the tag.

phrases.latin: Statim allātae sunt amphorae vitreae dīligenter gypsātae, quārum in cervīcibus pittacia erant affīxa cum hōc titulō: Falernum Opīmiānum annōrum centum.
phrases.english: At once glass jars, carefully sealed with plaster, were brought in, with labels fastened to their necks bearing this title: Falernian, Opimian vintage, a hundred years old.

sources: Lewis & Short: pittacium · Lewis & Short: titulus
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 25, s.v. etichetta.
